Generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape (GAMLSS) let each
parameter of a response distribution depend on covariates
[@Rigby+Stasinopoulos:2005]. The `gamlss2` package provides a workflow similar
to `lm()` and `glm()`, while allowing a separate additive predictor for every
distribution parameter.

We fit a seasonal model for motorcycle counts, inspect its effects and
residuals, and use the fitted distribution to estimate how often daily
traffic exceeds 500 motorcycles.

## Data

We use the `HarzTraffic` data included in the package. They contain daily
traffic counts and weather measurements near Sonnenberg in the Harz region of
Germany. Motorcycle traffic has a pronounced annual cycle, so we model the
number of motorcycles (`bikes`) as a smooth function of the day of the year
(`yday`, where January 1 is day 0).

```{r}
#| message: false
library("gamlss2")
data("HarzTraffic", package = "gamlss2")
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Daily motorcycle counts in the Harz region."
#| fig-alt: "Daily counts plotted against day of year, with higher motorcycle traffic in the middle of the year."
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(bikes ~ I(yday + 1), data = HarzTraffic,
  pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(1, 0.25),
  xlab = "Day of year", ylab = "Motorcycles")
```

The response is a count and its variance is much larger than its mean. We
therefore use the negative binomial `NBI` family. It has two parameters:
`mu`, the conditional mean, and `sigma`, a dispersion parameter. Both use a
log link.

## A first model

The first model lets the mean motorcycle count vary smoothly over the year.
The cyclic cubic spline (`bs = "cc"`) joins smoothly at the beginning and end
of the annual cycle.

```{r}
m1 <- gamlss2(
  bikes ~ s(yday, bs = "cc", k = 20),
  data = HarzTraffic,
  family = NBI,
  trace = FALSE
)
```

Only one right-hand side is supplied, so it is used for the first family
parameter, `mu`. The remaining parameter, `sigma`, receives an intercept-only
predictor. More generally, the right-hand sides separated by `|` correspond to
the family parameters in their displayed order:

| Formula | Interpretation for `NBI` |
|---|---|
| `bikes ~ x` | model `mu` with `x` and keep `sigma` constant |
| `bikes ~ x | z` | model `mu` with `x` and `sigma` with `z` |
| `bikes ~ x | .` | use the predictor `x` for both parameters |

Thus, a model in which both the mean and dispersion vary seasonally can be
specified compactly as follows.

```{r}
m2 <- gamlss2(
  bikes ~ s(yday, bs = "cc", k = 20) | .,
  data = HarzTraffic,
  family = NBI,
  trace = FALSE
)
```

For families with more parameters, further right-hand sides can be appended.
For example, `y ~ x | . | . | .` repeats the predictor for all four parameters
of a four-parameter family. Omitting right-hand sides instead gives the
remaining parameters intercept-only predictors.

## Inspecting the fitted model

The model summary reports the family and links, linear coefficients, effective
degrees of freedom of the smooth terms, and model-fit information.

```{r}
summary(m2)
```

Use `plot()` to inspect the seasonal effect on each parameter's log scale.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Estimated seasonal effects for the negative binomial mean and dispersion."
#| fig-alt: "Smooth effects of day of year on the log mean and log dispersion in separate panels."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1), cex = 1)
plot(m2, spar = FALSE)
par(op)
```

Normalized quantile residuals should be approximately standard normal when the
conditional distribution is well calibrated. Because randomized quantile
residuals are used for discrete distributions, we set a seed to make the plots
reproducible.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "In-sample diagnostics based on randomized quantile residuals."
#| fig-alt: "Four residual diagnostic plots for the seasonal negative binomial model."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7
set.seed(1328)
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1), cex = 1)
plot(m2, which = "resid", spar = FALSE)
par(op)
```

These are in-sample diagnostics. They can reveal important model deficiencies,
but do not by themselves establish out-of-sample calibration.

## Distributional predictions

We now evaluate the fitted seasonal cycle on each day of the year.

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(yday = 0:364)
```

By default, `predict()` returns a vector of fitted distributions using the
`distributions3` interface, with one distribution per row of `newdata`.

```{r}
pf <- predict(m2, newdata = nd)
head(pf)
```

Raw distribution parameters can be requested explicitly.

```{r}
parameters <- predict(m2, newdata = nd, type = "parameter")
head(parameters)
```

For example, the fitted probability of more than 500 motorcycles on a day is
$1 - F(500)$.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Fitted probability of more than 500 motorcycles by day of year."
#| fig-alt: "Curve showing how the fitted chance of exceeding 500 motorcycles varies over the year."
prob_high <- 1 - cdf(pf, 500)

par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(nd$yday + 1, prob_high, type = "l", lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Day of year",
  ylab = "Pr(Motorcycles > 500)")
```

Conditional quantiles follow directly from the predicted distributions. Here
we calculate the 5%, 50%, and 95% quantiles and add them to the observed counts.

```{r}
pq <- quantile(pf, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), elementwise = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Fitted 5th, 50th, and 95th percentiles of daily motorcycle counts."
#| fig-alt: "Observed daily counts with three seasonal percentile curves. The solid line is the median."
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(bikes ~ I(yday + 1), data = HarzTraffic,
  pch = 16, col = adjustcolor(1, 0.2),
  xlab = "Day of year", ylab = "Motorcycles")
matlines(nd$yday + 1, pq,
  lwd = 2, lty = c(3, 1, 2), col = 4)
legend("topright", c("5%", "50%", "95%"),
  lwd = 2, lty = c(3, 1, 2), col = 4, bty = "n")
```

The two outer curves bound a central 90% interval for daily counts under the
fitted model. The middle curve gives the fitted median on each day.

## Relation to `gamlss`

`gamlss2` is a fresh implementation of the GAMLSS framework, but it can also
use the family objects from
[`gamlss.dist`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=gamlss.dist).
Unlike the classic [`gamlss`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=gamlss) workflow,
`gamlss2()` supports [`mgcv`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mgcv)
smooth terms directly and uses the `|` notation to
place the predictors for all distribution parameters in a single formula.
